meldungen.titel: Consulting Deep Dive, part 10: the specialist boutiques, Simon-Kucher, Analysys Mason, zeb and Porsche Consulting
meldungen.text:
Not every serious consulting career starts at a generalist strategy house. A group of firms has built its reputation on a single lens, whether a function such as pricing, a sector such as telecoms or banking, or a method such as lean operations. They are smaller than MBB, they hire more specialised profiles, and the exits they open are correspondingly narrower but often deeper.

Simon-Kucher is the clearest example. Founded in Bonn, it is the global reference for pricing, monetisation and revenue management. In 2025 it grew revenue by six per cent to 606 million euros despite cautious client spending, and it now employs nearly 2,200 people in 45 offices across 32 countries. Growth came from its core pricing work and from digital and AI-related services. The firm is owned by more than 200 partners and led by co-CEOs Gunnar Clausen and Joerg Kruetten, a partnership model that keeps it independent of investors. Management Consulted describes the exit options as diverse: some alumni move to strategy boutiques or even MBB, many go into industry, typically into commercial, pricing or strategy roles where the skill of putting a number on willingness to pay is rare and highly valued.

Analysys Mason, which sits on your consulting list with a rating of 8, is the telecoms, media and technology specialist, headquartered in London. It runs two entry tracks: graduates either join the research team as Research Analysts, progressing to Senior and Principal Analyst, or enter the strategy consulting track as Associate Consultants, working on numerous projects for operators, regulators and investors in their first year. Its competitors on the research side are Gartner and IDC. One caveat matters here: neither the firm nor the guides consulted publish data on where its alumni land, so any claim about its exits would be speculation. Plausible destinations follow from the client base (operators, infrastructure funds, regulators), but they are not documented.

zeb, headquartered in Münster, is the specialist for banks and financial services in the German-speaking world, combining strategy, management and IT consulting. According to its own sustainability report, it generated 240 million euros of revenue in 2025 with more than 1,200 staff across Europe. You can join as an analyst after a bachelor's degree or as a consultant after a master's; the application process takes around six weeks and includes a case study. Strikingly, 31 per cent of its employees have been with the firm for more than six years, which suggests a culture where staying is as common as leaving. For exits, the logic is sector-bound: bank strategy departments, risk, finance and transformation roles in financial institutions.

Porsche Consulting, the carmaker's subsidiary, rounds out the group with an operations and lean-management profile; current headcount and revenue figures could not be verified for this issue, so they are left out rather than guessed.

The common pattern: boutiques give you a recognisable expertise early, which makes you attractive to employers who need exactly that skill, but they move you less easily into general management or private equity than MBB. A boutique makes most sense if you already know the function or sector you want to own.

meldungen.titel: Claude Artifacts can now be installed as desktop apps, while Anthropic's shares slip below their IPO price
meldungen.text:
Anthropic has introduced a beta feature that turns Claude Artifacts, the small interactive programs Claude builds in a chat, into standalone applications for macOS and Windows. You ask Claude to build something, click "Install as app", and from then on it sits in the dock or start menu and opens like any other program, without a line of code written by you. The feature requires the latest version of the Claude desktop app and is available on all plans, including free accounts; on Enterprise plans an owner must switch it on first.

The installed apps can do considerably more than an artifact in a browser tab. They can use your connectors and Claude itself, and with your permission they can send notifications, add a menu bar item, register global keyboard shortcuts, create transparent or always-on-top windows and call operating system interfaces. Anthropic's examples include custom terminals, file managers and video editors. There are limits: Docs, Slides and Sheets cannot be installed, you must be online and signed in for the apps to open, and every request an app sends to Claude counts towards your plan's usage limits. Anthropic does not review these apps before installation and advises granting full access only to apps you trust. According to Anthropic's Felix Rieseberg, anyone with an Apple Developer account can also have Claude build a fully standalone app.

The commercial backdrop is less cheerful. After three trading days the shares of the largest IPO in history have given back all their gains: on Tuesday Anthropic closed at 81.90 dollars, below the offering price of 83 dollars, after opening its first session at 111.50 and peaking at 115.10. On Monday, when Nvidia jumped 31.5 per cent on Jensen Huang's return, Anthropic was the only one of 20 major tech, AI and chip stocks to close lower. Investors, for now, prefer the hardware behind the AI boom to the labs building the models, and neither Claude Ship nor this launch has changed that.

meldungen.titel: Austria's new start-up fund of funds need only invest a fifth of its money at home
meldungen.text:
Austria's government wants its new fund of funds to turn domestic start-ups into scale-ups, yet the concept paper behind it allows most of the money to leave the country. The document from the office of State Secretary Elisabeth Zehetner (ÖVP), seen by Trending Topics, sets only a floor for the Austrian share: "at least the amount of the state anchor investment" must flow into Austrian companies. With up to 100 million euros of federal money and a target volume of 500 million, that is roughly 20 per cent. Up to 400 million euros could therefore go to funds, and through them to companies, outside Austria.

The vehicle, now called the Austrian Venture and Growth Fund of Funds, will not back start-ups directly. It invests in target funds, which in turn finance start-ups, scale-ups and spin-offs. To reach "market-standard return expectations" the paper calls for broad diversification and explicitly rules out restricting investments to Austria or Europe. The target funds themselves must be based in Europe and focus on key technologies, and funds with a defence component are possible. The annual return target is more than 10 per cent, which in practice means picking the most promising funds wherever they sit, and those funds mainly invest in their own regions. Even Austrian funds such as Speedinvest, the country's largest venture investor, describe themselves as pan-European.

At last Saturday's presentation, Zehetner and Finance Minister Markus Marterbauer (SPÖ) stayed vague: the fund would "invest internationally" but give "a strong boost to the domestic location", measured partly by capital that actually reaches Austrian companies. No concrete targets were given. The paper's argument is that locating the fund of funds in Austria will attract specialised scale-up funds that do not yet exist there, solving what it calls a "chicken and egg" problem, an effect it says has been seen in Israel and Denmark. A study by EcoAustria for the economics ministry supports a wide geographic focus, pointing to the well-documented home bias of venture funds: at Germany's KfW Capital, more than 90 per cent of portfolio companies are German without any formal quota.

Whether the plan works depends on who supplies the other 400 million euros. Erste Group and Uniqa already invest in funds of funds in Poland and at EU level but still see open questions in the Austrian model. Austria, according to the Atomico report, invests almost the least in start-ups relative to its economic output, and its start-ups currently depend almost entirely on foreign investors for larger rounds.

meldungen.titel: Kilmar Ábrego García leaves the United States for Spain, ending the most prominent deportation fight of Trump's second term
meldungen.text:
Kilmar Ábrego García, the Salvadoran man whose wrongful deportation became a symbol in the debate over President Donald Trump's immigration agenda, left the United States on Tuesday on a commercial flight from the Washington area to Madrid. Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, confirmed his departure, which The Hill described as a self-deportation. Ábrego García had been facing removal to one of several African countries proposed by the Department of Homeland Security.

The case has run for more than a year. Ábrego García entered the US illegally as a teenager, lived in Maryland and is married to a US citizen. In 2019 a judge barred his deportation to El Salvador because of the danger he faced from a gang there. In March 2025 the administration deported him anyway and he was held in Cecot, El Salvador's notoriously harsh mega-prison. The Supreme Court then upheld an order requiring the government to "facilitate" his return. The administration admitted the error and brought him back in June, but indicted him on human smuggling charges linked to a 2022 traffic stop. In May a federal judge dismissed the case as vindictive; the Justice Department has appealed. Officials accused him of membership in the MS-13 gang, which he denies. When reports emerged that the government wanted to send him to Uganda, a judge barred deportation to a third country; Costa Rica had offered him refugee status.

Van Hollen called the outcome an agreement the administration "was forced to" accept, one that respects Ábrego García's will and due process. His lawyer described the departure as temporary and said the family expects a future administration to allow his return. The BBC said it had asked the Department of Homeland Security for comment.

The episode ends without a court resolving the central legal questions about third-country removals, and the appeal over the dismissed indictment remains formally pending.

meldungen.titel: Germany: Klingbeil wants to close the share deal loophole in real estate transfer tax, but his draft puts no number on the gain
meldungen.text:
The decision. German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil (SPD) has circulated a draft bill, seen by Reuters on Tuesday, to tighten the rules on so-called share deals from 1 July 2027. In a share deal the buyer does not purchase a building or plot directly but the shares of the company that owns it. Because no property formally changes hands, the Grunderwerbsteuer (real estate transfer tax), which ranges from 3.5 to 6.5 per cent of the price depending on the state, often does not apply. Under the draft, several buyers who together acquire at least 90 per cent of a property-owning company could trigger the tax, and new legal terms would define who actually controls the shares. At the same time, intra-group restructurings would be eased. The draft still needs agreement within the government, and associations have not yet been consulted.

The case made. The ministry argues that the 2021 reform did not fully work and that "in certain areas" there is still a need to legislate. It expects fewer tax-driven structures and more ordinary property transfers, which would raise revenue for the states, who receive the tax. Critics come from a different angle: the owners' association Haus und Grund says the draft offers nothing to first-time buyers. "With a purchase price of 400,000 euros and a tax rate of 6.5 per cent, the transfer tax alone comes to 26,000 euros," it calculated, and wants owner-occupying first-time buyers exempted.

The numbers. Transfer tax revenue for the states reached 15.1 billion euros in 2025, up from 12.75 billion in 2024, but still well below the 2021 peak of 18.3 billion (Immowelt). The only published estimate of what share deals cost is about one billion euros a year, a DIW figure from July 2021 cited in a Green motion in the Bundestag (Drucksache 21/6646, June 2026); it predates the effect of the 2021 reform. The draft itself quantifies only one item: the relief for corporate restructurings, at roughly 75 million euros a year in lost revenue. It contains no estimate of the additional revenue from closing the loophole.

Reality check. The claim that share deals still erode the tax base is plausible and supported by the 2021 DIW order of magnitude, which would equal roughly 7 per cent of 2025 revenue. But the ministry's own expectation of higher revenue is not backed by any figure, so the net effect is unknown: the only number in the draft is a cost. Haus und Grund's arithmetic is correct for a 6.5 per cent state, but whether first-time buyers should be exempted is a value judgement and a separate policy question that the data cannot settle. Missing entirely is current evidence on how many transactions still use share deals since 2021.

Evidence rating: Thinly grounded. The direction is consistent with an older estimate, but the draft quantifies its cost and not its central promised benefit.
